body.text: Across Southeast Asia, air forces are racing to modernize, but Indonesia and Singapore have taken very different paths in upgrading their combat aircraft fleets. The former is expanding its supplier base, while the latter is doubling down on U.S. platforms. Both approaches promise strategic advantages, but each carries a distinct vulnerability. Buying advanced fighters is one thing; keeping them combat-ready is another.
Indonesia and Over-Diversification

Indonesia currently operates Western aircraft: American F-16s, British Hawk 109/209 aircraft, and French Rafales. It also operates Russian Su-27 and Su-30 fighters and the South Korean T-50i. Future procurements will likely include the Turkish KAAN, South Korean KF-21, and Chinese J-10.

This approach serves Indonesia’s strategic interests. First, it reflects Indonesia’s longstanding desire for strategic autonomy, shaped by its “free and active” foreign policy principle. Diversifying suppliers gives Jakarta diplomatic flexibility, allowing it to maintain defense relationships with multiple powers rather than depend too heavily on one.

Such diversity may broaden Indonesia’s diplomatic options and reduce the vulnerability of its defense supply chain. If no single supplier dominates Indonesia’s defense tech, no one can leverage a monopoly to influence or shape Indonesia’s foreign or defense policy.

Historical events reinforce Indonesia’s need to maintain relations with multiple powers while avoiding reliance on any one supplier for defense. From the late 1990s to the early 2000s, the United States and its European allies imposed an arms embargo on Indonesia, which included sales of munitions and military equipment, in the aftermath of violence in East Timor, which was then part of Indonesia.

Defense officials recognize the potential consequences of arms embargoes for military readiness and the need to procure aircraft suited to the operational scenarios Indonesia’s air force is likely to face. At the same time, conversations with Indonesian defense officials over the years, particularly those in the air force, suggest that Jakarta is also aware of the risks of supplier diversification, including the dangers of over-diversification.

A meeting I had with a group of senior Indonesian military officials more than a year ago offered further insight into this thinking. One official acknowledged the drawbacks of operating multiple aircraft types but explained that Indonesia’s acquisition strategy was also driven by a basic operational requirement: ensuring the air force had a minimum number of modern combat aircraft to cover and defend an archipelago spanning thousands of islands. In this context, diversification is not simply about expanding strategic options; it is also an attempt to address the challenge of generating sufficient air power across an enormous geographic area.

Crucially, the official added that Indonesia expected its air force, at least in the short and medium term, to focus more on counterinsurgency operations than on air-to-air combat against external adversaries. This operational assessment helps explain why interoperability was not a leading consideration in selecting new combat aircraft.

The logic is not without merit. Indonesia continues to grapple with an armed insurgency in West Papua, making internal security missions an important consideration in its assessment of future air power requirements.

The Indonesian Air Force will likely at one point in time operate eight different types of combat aircraft from a broad range of suppliers – Western, Chinese, Korean, Russian, and Turkish. What are the drawbacks of having too many different suppliers?

Overdiversification of its fleet is likely to complicate the Indonesian Air Force’s ability to generate effective combat air power. Interoperability is one challenge: integrating aircraft from different countries can complicate joint operations, as Russian Sukhois or Chinese J-10s may face technical and operational barriers when operating alongside U.S. F-16s or French Rafales.

Financing presents another challenge. Each additional aircraft type creates long-term costs that extend well beyond the initial purchase, including separate maintenance arrangements, technical training, spare-parts inventories, weapons integration, and logistical support. Without economies of scale, these competing demands can drive up operating costs, stretch Indonesia’s defense budget and undermine the operational benefits that diversification is intended to deliver.

The consequences are particularly evident in the Indonesian Air Force’s limited acquisition of air-to-air munitions. Data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) indicates that Indonesia has acquired relatively few missiles for its combat aircraft over the past 25 years. For example, it acquired just 36 U.S. AIM-120C AMRAAM missiles for its F-16 fleet. Such a limited inventory raises serious questions about the air force’s ability to sustain air combat operations during a prolonged conflict against an external adversary.
Having a diverse fleet of modern combat aircraft means little if the air force cannot adequately arm and sustain them.
Singapore: An American-centric Approach?

While Indonesia relies on a broad range of suppliers, Singapore has taken a different path. It has doubled down on U.S.-built platforms. The Republic of Singapore Air Force’s modernization program has prioritized advanced platforms, networked capabilities, and integration with a wider ecosystem of primarily U.S. military technology. Its F-16s and F-15SGs provide established combat capabilities, while its planned fleet of F-35As and F-35Bs will strengthen stealth and the ability to operate in contested environments. Singapore’s first F-35 is scheduled for delivery by the end of 2026.

This approach offers considerable advantages. By focusing on a smaller number of sophisticated, highly integrated platforms, the air force can invest in high-quality training and integrate aircraft with airborne early-warning and command-and-control capabilities, enabling it to develop common operating pictures and shorten the sensor-to-shooter cycle.
Yet this model comes with a strategic vulnerability: over-reliance on the United States for critical aircraft, advanced weapons, software, maintenance, and training support.

This dependence does not mean Washington can automatically dictate Singapore’s foreign policy or switch off its aircraft at will. Singapore retains considerable agency and has cultivated a strong defense relationship with the United States over decades. Nevertheless, U.S. export controls, political decisions and supply-chain disruptions could affect the availability of equipment, upgrades, and munitions.

The concern is especially relevant when demand for U.S. weapon platforms and spare parts rises sharply across multiple theaters. Singapore could find itself competing with the United States’ own forces and U.S. allies for scarce resources.

One example is the limited operational deployment of the F-35Bs Singapore purchased. Singapore purchased them in 2019 because their STOVL capability suits Singapore’s limited land space and offers operational flexibility. More importantly, dispersed operations could reduce reliance on vulnerable fixed air bases, strengthening the Singaporean air force’s resilience and ability to sustain air power during conflicts.

However, these F-35Bs are being based permanently at Ebbing Air National Guard Base in Arkansas, United States. Publicly available evidence does not suggest Washington required Singapore to base its F-35Bs in the United States as a condition of sale. However, U.S. arms sales to foreign buyers often include conditions on deployment or storage.

Permanently deploying F-35Bs in the United States could undermine Singapore’s original rationale for the acquisition. Therefore, Singapore’s heavy reliance on U.S. combat aircraft could prove to be an Achilles’ heel in any military conflict. Washington could restrict the operational use of Singapore’s entire fleet of combat aircraft, which rely solely on U.S. platforms, potentially constraining Singapore’s ability to defend itself effectively and independently.
Acquisition vs Operation

Indonesia’s and Singapore’s experiences show that neither diversification nor concentration is inherently superior. The effectiveness of either strategy depends on whether procurement decisions support an effective and sustainable military campaign when the time comes.

Indonesia must ensure that strategic autonomy does not become logistical fragmentation. Its acquisitions of the French and Turkish combat aircraft, for example, can strengthen its capabilities. But Indonesia should also assess the commitments against funding, maintenance capacity, and weapon availability.

Singapore, meanwhile, must ensure that its sophisticated U.S. platforms do not become a single point of strategic vulnerability. Its priority should be to preserve operational independence within a defense partnership on which it heavily relies.

Ultimately, these two Southeast Asian states must recognize that military strength depends not simply on the platforms they acquire, but on their ability to sustain, operate, and employ them as and when security circumstances demand.
